name: Transcendentalism
line: Simplify. Live deliberately, close to nature.

quote.text: I went to the woods because I wished to live deliberately, to front only the essential facts of life.

quotes.text: Trust thyself: every heart vibrates to that iron string.
In the woods, we return to reason and faith.
Our life is frittered away by detail. Simplicity, simplicity, simplicity!
Very early, I knew that the only object in life was to grow.
In Wildness is the preservation of the World.
If a man does not keep pace with his companions, perhaps it is because he hears a different drummer.

words.meaning: Trust in your own mind and conscience
words.usage: The title of Emerson’s 1841 essay. Not self-sufficiency: fidelity to your own perception.

words.meaning: The shared spirit within and beyond every person
words.usage: That unity within which every particular being is contained and made one with all others.

words.meaning: Known by intuition, beyond what the senses give
words.usage: The name was first used to mock the group. They kept it.

words.meaning: The faculty that sees truth directly
words.usage: Opposed to the Understanding, which only calculates and compares.

words.meaning: Primary wisdom, before teaching
words.usage: Emerson: we denote this primary wisdom as Intuition, whilst all later teachings are tuitions.

words.meaning: With full attention and by choice
words.usage: The key word of Walden. From the Latin for weighing.

words.meaning: Fewer things, more life
words.usage: Thoreau: let your affairs be as two or three, and not a hundred or a thousand.

words.meaning: The real cost of things, counted in life
words.usage: The first and longest chapter of Walden. The cost of a thing is the amount of life exchanged for it.

words.meaning: Walking as a practice, without errand
words.usage: Thoreau fancifully derives it from pilgrims going à la Sainte Terre, to the Holy Land.

words.meaning: The untamed, in nature and in the mind
words.usage: Not the same as wilderness. Thoreau found it in a swamp at the edge of town.

words.meaning: Refusing the crowd’s script
words.usage: Emerson: whoso would be a man must be a nonconformist.

words.meaning: Nature as a mirror of the mind
words.usage: Every natural fact is a symbol of some spiritual fact.

words.meaning: Everything that is not the soul
words.usage: His definition of nature: all that is separate from us, including one’s own body.

words.meaning: The self dissolved in seeing
words.usage: "I am nothing; I see all." The most quoted and most teased image in Nature.

words.meaning: Conscience, above statute
words.usage: What one obeys when the law of the land requires injustice.

words.meaning: Openly refusing an unjust law and accepting the penalty
words.usage: The later title of Thoreau’s 1849 essay.

words.meaning: The inner voice of right
words.usage: Thoreau: must the citizen resign his conscience to the legislator? Why has every man a conscience, then?

words.meaning: The lifelong cultivation of one’s powers
words.usage: From the Unitarian William Ellery Channing. The German word is Bildung.

words.meaning: The voice of one’s own nature
words.usage: Emerson: to believe that what is true for you in your private heart is true for all, that is genius.

words.meaning: The balance that runs through all things
words.usage: An Emerson essay: every excess causes a defect, every defect an excess.

words.meaning: Every truth is surrounded by a larger one
words.usage: An Emerson essay. Around every circle another can be drawn.

words.meaning: A hall for public lectures
words.usage: How Emerson earned his living, town by town, for forty years.

words.meaning: Guided discussion as a method of education
words.usage: Margaret Fuller’s paid "Conversations" for Boston women, 1839 to 1844.

words.meaning: A notebook of passages copied from one’s reading
words.usage: Both men kept them alongside their journals.

words.meaning: The daily record of observation and thought
words.usage: Thoreau’s runs to some two million words. Emerson called his a savings bank.

words.meaning: Wandering beyond the usual bounds
words.usage: From the Latin for wandering outside. He feared his writing was not extra-vagant enough.

words.meaning: Fully alive to the present
words.usage: Thoreau: to be awake is to be alive. I have never yet met a man who was quite awake.

words.meaning: Being alone without being lonely
words.usage: A chapter of Walden: I never found the companion that was so companionable as solitude.

words.meaning: Grass-ground river
words.usage: The name the area’s first people gave the Concord River. Thoreau used it.

words.meaning: Going out to pick wild berries
words.usage: Thoreau led the town’s children on berry-picking parties and thought it an education.

words.meaning: Changing society by first changing oneself
words.usage: They argued about which comes first, and joined abolition either way.

words.meaning: A calling; the work that is yours
words.usage: Emerson: each man has his own vocation. The talent is the call.

practices.name: Morning pages
practices.instructions: Before reading anything, write by hand for fifteen minutes. Begin with what you observe: the light, the weather, the state of your mind. Then follow whatever thought is most alive. Do not edit and do not write for a reader. Date the entry.
practices.why: Emerson asked the young Thoreau, "Do you keep a journal?" and Thoreau began one that day and kept it for twenty-four years. The phrase "morning pages" is modern. The habit of writing at dawn is theirs.
variations: Start with one precise observation from the window.
Copy a sentence from yesterday’s reading and answer it.

practices.name: Saunter
practices.instructions: Walk for an hour without a phone, a route or a purpose. Go toward whatever is least built: a park, a river, a field edge. Let the walking set the thinking. If your mind stays in the office, notice that your body has gone for a walk without you, and call it back.
practices.why: Thoreau wrote that he could not keep his health and spirits without at least four hours a day sauntering through woods and fields, absolutely free from worldly engagements.
variations: Walk the same path all week and note what changes.
Walk before dawn or after dark.
Walk in whatever direction you have never gone.

practices.name: Read aloud
practices.instructions: Read a few pages of Walden, an Emerson essay or a Whitman poem aloud, slowly enough to hear the sentences. Mark one passage. Read it again and ask whether you believe it.
practices.why: These are spoken texts. Emerson’s essays began as lectures, and Thoreau’s Walden was delivered in the Concord Lyceum before it was a book.
variations: Read to someone else and talk about it afterwards.

practices.name: Nature journal
practices.instructions: Record what you saw in the natural world today, with the date: which plants are in leaf or flower, which birds, what the sky did, the temperature, the first or last of anything. Be exact. Sketch if you like. Leave out your opinions.
practices.why: In his last decade Thoreau filled his journal with dated records of when each plant flowered and each bird arrived around Concord. Scientists now use them to measure how the climate has shifted.
variations: Follow one tree or one patch of ground.
Record first sightings of the season.
Note sunrise and sunset times and what the moon is doing.

rules.why: Thinking, for them, was done on foot and in weather.
A man is rich in proportion to the number of things which he can afford to let alone.
Thoreau on the telegraph: we are in great haste to connect Maine and Texas, but Maine and Texas, it may be, have nothing important to communicate.

rules.text: Trust one decision of your own
rules.why: Self-reliance is practiced in small acts: say what you think, choose without polling.
Emerson: speak what you think now in hard words, and tomorrow speak what tomorrow thinks, though it contradict everything you said today.

rules.text: Do not cooperate with what you believe is wrong
rules.why: The lesson of Thoreau’s night in jail. Start small and close to home.

eat.title: Bread and beans
eat.creator: Baked beans, unleavened bread
eat.why: Thoreau hoed seven miles of bean rows and baked his bread on a shingle over the fire.

eat.title: Berries
eat.creator: Picked yourself if possible
eat.why: He thought a huckleberry never reaches Boston: the essence is lost in the cart.

eat.title: A simple one-pot meal
eat.creator: Rice, beans, vegetables
eat.why: His food at the pond cost him about twenty-seven cents a week.

eat.title: Apples
eat.creator: An old variety
eat.why: His late essay "Wild Apples" praises the sour, uncultivated ones.

drink.title: Water
drink.creator: From a spring or the tap
drink.why: Thoreau: I believe that water is the only drink for a wise man.

drink.title: Herbal tea
drink.creator: From something that grows near you

drink.title: Sweet cider
drink.creator: Fresh-pressed apple
drink.why: The drink of a New England autumn.

customs.title: Keep a journal
customs.creator: Daily
customs.why: Emerson and Thoreau both wrote in theirs almost every day of their adult lives.

customs.title: Walk four hours
customs.creator: Thoreau’s ideal
customs.why: Or as close as your day allows.

customs.title: Read in the open air
customs.creator: Take a book outside
customs.why: He kept Homer on his table at the pond.

customs.title: Three chairs
customs.creator: One for solitude, two for friendship, three for society
customs.why: How Thoreau furnished his house. Invite one person for real conversation.

customs.title: Keep an account
customs.creator: Of what you spend and why
customs.why: Walden lists the cost of the house to the half cent: twenty-eight dollars, twelve and a half cents.

customs.title: Go to a lecture
customs.creator: And talk about it afterwards
customs.why: The lyceum was their internet. Listen to one long talk in company.

ethics.title: Trust thyself
ethics.text: Believe your own thought. The conviction in your private heart, honestly held, is your contribution. Imitation is suicide.
ethics.practice: Give your real opinion once today where you would normally hedge.

ethics.title: Live deliberately
ethics.text: Choose what you do and know why. Do not arrive at death and discover you had not lived.
ethics.practice: Before one habitual act today, ask whether you chose it.

ethics.title: Obey conscience over law
ethics.text: When the law requires you to be the agent of injustice to another, break the law. The only obligation is to do what you think right.
ethics.practice: Find one small complicity and withdraw from it.

ethics.title: Simplify
ethics.text: Each possession and commitment costs life. Keep the ones worth the price.
ethics.practice: Remove one obligation or one object this week.

ethics.title: Self-culture
ethics.text: Your first duty is to become fully yourself, because that is what you have to give.
ethics.practice: Spend an hour today on what develops you, not on what is urgent.

ethics.title: Act on principle
ethics.text: They moved from essays to the Underground Railroad. A belief that costs nothing is only an opinion.
ethics.practice: Do one concrete thing for a cause you say you care about.

philosophy.title: Nature as teacher
philosophy.text: The natural world is not scenery. Attended to closely, it instructs: in patience, in economy, in the laws of your own mind.
philosophy.practice: Watch one natural process for ten minutes and write what it teaches.

philosophy.title: Self-reliance
philosophy.text: Society is in conspiracy against the independence of each of its members. The virtue most in request is conformity. Self-reliance is its aversion.
philosophy.practice: Notice one thing you do only because others do.

philosophy.title: Simplicity
philosophy.text: Most of what we call necessities are not. Reduce your wants and you buy back your time.
philosophy.practice: List what you truly need for a good day. It will be short.

philosophy.title: The Oversoul
philosophy.text: One mind is common to all individual people. In quiet you can feel that the deepest thing in you is not private.
philosophy.practice: Sit in silence for ten minutes and listen for what is not your chatter.

philosophy.title: The infinitude of the private person
philosophy.text: Emerson said he had taught one doctrine: the infinitude of the private man. Each person has direct access to truth.
philosophy.practice: Take one of your own unspoken ideas seriously today.

philosophy.title: Correspondence
philosophy.text: The laws of nature and the laws of the mind answer to each other. A fact fully seen becomes a metaphor.
philosophy.practice: Find in today’s weather a picture of your own state.

philosophy.title: The present
philosophy.text: These roses under my window make no reference to former roses. They exist with God today. Only man postpones and remembers.
philosophy.practice: Give one hour to exactly what is in front of you.

philosophy.title: Compensation
philosophy.text: Nothing is got for nothing. Every gain has its price and every loss its gift.
philosophy.practice: Name the hidden cost of something you wanted and got.

philosophy.title: Wildness
philosophy.text: Life consists with wildness. The most alive is the wildest. What is tame in you is what has gone dead.

philosophy.title: Awakening
philosophy.text: Most people are half asleep. To be awake is to be alive, and it takes practice every morning.
philosophy.practice: Tomorrow, greet the dawn on your feet.

Where did you follow the crowd, and where yourself?
What could you remove from your life?
What felt most alive today?
What did your walk give you?
What did you buy, or want to buy, and why?

What did you leave unsaid?
What is the true cost of something you own?

What did the morning look like?
Which sentence from your reading stayed with you?
Where did you imitate?
What does your conscience say about how you earn or spend?
What did the weather teach you?
What would you do if you needed no one’s approval?
What is flowering, fruiting or fading where you live?
What did solitude give you? What did company give you?
What habit is living your life for you?
What law, rule or custom are you obeying against your judgement?
What is enough?
Which of your possessions owns you?
What did you do today only for its own sake?
Where do you feel most yourself?
What would you do with one more free hour a day?
What did you learn from a person you disagree with?
What are you postponing?
What wild thing is left in you?
What do you believe that you have never tested?
What are you living for?
reflect: What did living deliberately show you about your ordinary days?
Which practice changed you the most, and why?
Where did you resist, and what was the resistance protecting?
What did you remove, and do you miss it?
Where did you trust yourself, and what happened?
What will you keep, now that you are leaving the woods?

intro: Transcendentalism was a movement of writers, ministers and reformers in New England in the 1830s and 1840s who held that every person has direct access to truth, through intuition and through nature, and need not take it second-hand from church, state or custom.

It began as a revolt inside Unitarianism, the liberal religion of Boston’s educated class. To a group of young ministers it had become, in Emerson’s phrase, corpse-cold: reasonable, respectable and without fire. Reading the German idealists, the English Romantics and newly translated Hindu and Buddhist scriptures, they concluded that the mind is not a blank page written on by the senses. It has a higher faculty, which they called Reason, that perceives spiritual truth at first hand. In 1836 Ralph Waldo Emerson, who had resigned his own pulpit, published a small book called Nature that asked: why should not we also enjoy an original relation to the universe?

Around Emerson in the village of Concord gathered a remarkable company. Margaret Fuller edited their magazine, The Dial, and wrote the first great American argument for the equality of women. Bronson Alcott ran experimental schools and a short-lived vegan commune. Elizabeth Peabody published them and opened the country’s first English-language kindergarten. Theodore Parker preached to thousands. And Henry David Thoreau, a pencil-maker’s son fourteen years Emerson’s junior, built a one-room house on Emerson’s land by Walden Pond and lived there for two years, two months and two days, to find out how much of what people call necessary he could do without.

They did not agree on everything, and they cheerfully admitted to having no system. What they shared were a few convictions. Nature is a teacher and a text, to be read with close attention. The individual conscience outranks any institution. Conformity is a kind of death. A simple life leaves room for a real one. And ideas are worthless until lived, which is why the movement produced experiments: Brook Farm, Fruitlands, the cabin at the pond.

It also produced resistance. Thoreau went to jail for a night rather than pay a tax to a government that upheld slavery, and wrote the essay later called Civil Disobedience, which Gandhi and Martin Luther King Jr. both acknowledged. By the 1850s nearly all of them were active abolitionists, sheltering fugitives and defending John Brown.

This Onda follows Thoreau’s method more than Emerson’s theory: write at dawn, walk for an hour, read something worth reading aloud, record the natural world exactly, buy little and decide for yourself. It asks one question for a few weeks: what is essential?

figures.name: Ralph Waldo Emerson
figures.bio: Former minister, essayist and lecturer. The movement’s centre of gravity.

figures.name: Henry David Thoreau
figures.bio: Writer, naturalist, surveyor and tax resister. Author of Walden.

figures.name: Margaret Fuller
figures.bio: Critic, editor of The Dial and foreign correspondent. Died in a shipwreck returning from Italy.

figures.name: Bronson Alcott
figures.bio: Educator and idealist. Founder of the Temple School and of Fruitlands. Father of Louisa May.

figures.name: Elizabeth Palmer Peabody
figures.bio: Bookseller, publisher and educator. Her Boston shop was the movement’s meeting place.

figures.name: Theodore Parker
figures.bio: Radical minister and abolitionist whose phrases were later echoed by Lincoln and by King.

figures.name: Walt Whitman
figures.bio: Poet of Leaves of Grass. "I was simmering, simmering, simmering; Emerson brought me to a boil."

figures.name: Louisa May Alcott
figures.bio: Author of Little Women. Grew up among the Transcendentalists and satirised them fondly.

figures.name: Frederic Henry Hedge
figures.bio: Scholar of German philosophy. The Transcendental Club was first called Hedge’s Club.

history.what: Nature is published and the Transcendental Club first meets
history.detail: Emerson’s book appears anonymously in September. The same month a group of ministers and friends begins meeting in Boston and Concord to talk philosophy.
Emerson’s address at Harvard calls for an end to dependence on European thought. It was later called America’s intellectual declaration of independence.
Emerson tells the graduating ministers to find God in themselves and not in historical miracles. Harvard does not invite him back for nearly thirty years.
The movement’s quarterly, edited first by Margaret Fuller and then by Emerson, runs for four years.
Emerson’s first series of essays includes Self-Reliance and The Over-Soul. George Ripley founds a cooperative farm at West Roxbury that lasts until 1847.
Bronson Alcott and Charles Lane start a commune using no animal products or animal labour. It collapses within seven months.
He moves in on the Fourth of July. Margaret Fuller publishes Woman in the Nineteenth Century the same year.
Thoreau is arrested for refusing the poll tax, in protest at slavery and the war with Mexico. Someone pays it and he is released next morning, to his annoyance.
The lecture on his night in jail is published. It is later retitled Civil Disobedience.

history.what: The Fugitive Slave Act, and the death of Fuller
history.detail: The law requiring northerners to return escaped slaves turns the group toward open resistance. Fuller drowns off Fire Island with her husband and child in July.
After seven drafts. It sells slowly. The same summer Thoreau delivers "Slavery in Massachusetts".
Whitman sends a copy to Emerson, who replies: I greet you at the beginning of a great career.
Of tuberculosis, on 6 May, aged forty-four. Asked whether he had made his peace with God, he is said to have answered that he was not aware they had ever quarrelled.
On 27 April, in Concord. He is buried on Authors’ Ridge in Sleepy Hollow Cemetery, near Thoreau, Hawthorne and the Alcotts.

concepts.text: Truth is perceived directly by each person.
concepts.detail: They took Kant’s word "transcendental", for what the mind brings to experience, and stretched it to mean a faculty of spiritual insight. Scripture and custom are at best reports of someone else’s intuition.

concepts.text: The visible world as a language of spirit.
concepts.detail: Emerson gives nature four uses: commodity, beauty, language and discipline. Thoreau turned the theory into practice, measuring the pond and recording when each flower opened.
Not rugged individualism. It rests on the claim that the deepest self is shared, so that to be truly oneself is to be in touch with what is universal.

concepts.text: The one mind in which all individuals share.
concepts.detail: Emerson’s name for the divine as an indwelling presence, influenced by his reading of the Upaniṣads and Plotinus.

concepts.text: Counting the cost of things in life.
concepts.detail: Walden’s first chapter is a household budget and an argument: most people spend their lives earning what they do not need.
Under a government which imprisons any unjustly, the true place for a just man is also a prison. The idea travelled to Gandhi in South Africa and to the American civil rights movement.

concepts.text: The duty of unfolding one’s nature.
concepts.detail: Education is drawing out, not putting in. Fuller’s Conversations and Alcott’s schools tried to practise it.
They disagreed over whether to reform society or the self first. In practice they did both.

concepts.text: Ideas must be tried in living.
concepts.detail: Thoreau called his time at Walden an experiment. He left when it was done, saying he had several more lives to live.
John Muir, the national parks, Whitman and Dickinson, pragmatism and the nature essay all descend from Concord.

facts.text: Thoreau’s house at Walden measured ten feet by fifteen and cost him twenty-eight dollars, twelve and a half cents.
Walden Pond is a mile and a half from Concord centre. Thoreau walked into town most days and often dined with family and friends. He never claimed to be a hermit.
He took a copy of the Bhagavad Gītā to the pond and wrote that in the morning he bathed his intellect in its philosophy.
The Thoreau family made the best pencils in America. Henry improved the graphite process that made them so.
Scientists have used Thoreau’s records of flowering dates in the 1850s to show that spring in Concord now arrives much earlier.
Gandhi read Civil Disobedience in South Africa and said it left a deep impression on him.
Louisa May Alcott’s satire of the Fruitlands commune is titled Transcendental Wild Oats.
Concord’s river was called Musketaquid by the Algonquian-speaking people who lived there first. The land around Walden is their homeland.
